clue.text: Head off to relax around start of parliamentary recess

indicators.note: the shortened word is placed around the initial, which sits within it
the first letter of the word for relax is cut away, as a head is removed

parts.note: to relax is to ease off

indicators.note: the opening letter of parliamentary is all that is used

explanation.surface: A weary MP is told to unwind just as Parliament breaks for its holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' trims EASE to ASE, and 'around' puts that round P, the first letter of 'parliamentary'. 'Recess' looks like a parliamentary holiday, but here it means an alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular recess at the end of a church, so the architectural sense of recess fits.

clue.text: American chaps occupy divine spot

indicators.note: the American men take up residence inside the word for divine

parts.note: to divine is to foretell or forecast
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Some Americans take over a holy site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' reads as an adjective with 'spot', a holy place, but it is a verb; 'occupy' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot, as in a tight spot, is an awkward situation or dilemma.

clue.text: Making soft pork pie in Melton? That's unusual

indicators.note: the fib is placed in among the reworked town letters
unusual signals that the letters of Melton are to be rearranged

parts.note: pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie

explanation.surface: Melton Mowbray is famous for pork pies, so a softening pie from there would be odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' shuffles the town into EMOLNT, which 'in' opens up. Melton Mowbray is an English town famous for its pork pies, and 'pork pie' is Cockney rhyming slang.
explanation.definitionFit: An emollient substance soothes and softens skin, so it is something making soft.

clue.text: After wasting little time, decide case that's cut and dried

indicators.note: the pieces are wasted, ruined and jumbled, before reassembling

parts.note: T is the usual abbreviation for time
taken as written

indicators.note: cut takes the final letter off the word case

parts.note: taken as written, less its tail

explanation.surface: A judge, after dawdling, rules on a case that turns out to be straightforward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims the last letter, giving CAS, and 'After wasting' shuffles the pool. 'Cut and dried' looks like one phrase meaning settled, but 'dried' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiccated food has had its moisture removed, so it is a synonym for dried.

clue.text: One called up doctor, needing back pills

parts.note: aft means at the back, as on a ship
E is slang for an ecstasy pill, so two of them are pills

explanation.surface: A patient phones the doctor because they need their pills back.
explanation.walkthrough: E is slang for a tablet of the drug ecstasy, so EE is plural pills.
explanation.definitionFit: A conscript is called up for military service, an American term for one drafted.

clue.text: What makes match so sickening?

parts.note: the first word is an anagram of the letters of match so, and the second word is the signal that churns them

explanation.surface: Someone asks what made a sporting contest so nauseating to watch.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay and STOMACH churned, mixed up, gives MATCH SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that turns the stomach is nauseating, so the hyphenated adjective means sickening.

clue.text: Lament having smashed last glass

parts.note: to lament is to cry

indicators.note: smashed signals that the letters of last are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone weeps after breaking the final glass of a set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smashed' rearranges the second word into STAL. 'Glass' looks like the object broken, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Crystal is fine, high-quality glass, as in crystal decanters and wine glasses.

clue.text: Figure of speech seen in poet's last line

indicators.note: last picks out only the final letter of the word poet's, ignoring the apostrophe

parts.note: a rope is a line, as on a ship

explanation.surface: A literary device appears in the final line of a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' takes T, the final letter of 'poet's'. 'Line' looks like a line of verse, but here it is a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figurative or metaphorical use of a word, a kind of figure of speech.

clue.text: Wild dog, canine at heart?

indicators.note: wild signals that the letters that follow are to be scrambled
at heart picks out the two central letters of canine

explanation.surface: A wild dog is, deep down, still a canine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at heart' takes NI, the middle of 'canine', and 'Wild' shuffles DOG + NI. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian wild dog is a canine, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Disparaging past socialist turned Conservative

indicators.note: turned means these two words are read backwards

parts.note: ago means in the past
red is a common label for a socialist
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A sneering remark about a former left-winger who became a Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses AGO + RED to make DEROGA. 'Turned' looks like the socialist changing sides, but it is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Derogatory remarks belittle or disparage, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Sellers perhaps talk a lot

definitions.meaning: Peter Sellers was a member of the ... Show comedy team, so he is an example

explanation.surface: Salespeople, perhaps, tend to be chatty.
explanation.walkthrough: The Goon Show was a 1950s British radio comedy starring Peter Sellers, Spike Milligan and Harry Secombe. 'Sellers' looks like salespeople, but it is the comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Sellers was one of the radio comedy's stars, and to drone on means talk a lot.

clue.text: Cocktail of gin taken primarily with lime

definitions.text: Cocktail of gin taken primarily with lime

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters that follow are mixed up
primarily takes the opening letter of gin and of taken

explanation.surface: A drink recipe: mostly gin, with lime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' takes G and T, the first letters of 'gin' and 'taken', and 'Cocktail of' mixes them with LIME. The whole clue also describes the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The gimlet is a classic cocktail of gin and lime cordial, exactly as the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Intimate friend first to entrust with key therefore to house

parts.note: Alt is a key on a computer keyboard

indicators.note: the Latin word takes in the initial letter, housing it

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore

indicators.note: first to takes just the opening letter of entrust

explanation.surface: A close friend is the first you would trust with your house key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to' takes the initial of 'entrust', and 'to house' sets it inside the Latin word. 'Key' is a computer key, not a door key.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally another self, the phrase is used for a very close and trusted friend.

clue.text: Threaten to go out and shoot street urchin

parts.note: a candle flame that gutters flickers and threatens to go out
to snipe is to shoot from cover

explanation.surface: A street kid is threatened with being shot unless they leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threaten to go out' looks like a threat to someone, but it describes a flickering candle.
explanation.definitionFit: A guttersnipe is a ragged child of the streets, an old word for a street urchin.

clue.text: Food from Japan, say?

definitions.meaning: the meals served, as on a menu
Japan is an example of a Far Eastern country, written as a word for distant plus E for east

explanation.surface: A question about whether a dish is Japanese.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as an abbreviation for Far East, which Japan is part of; the question mark shows Japan is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Food served at a meal or on a menu is the fare, as in simple country fare.

clue.text: I hear latex is kinky, providing thrill

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of these words are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone has heard that rubber clothing is a turn-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kinky' looks like a description of latex, but it is the signal to rearrange I HEAR LATEX.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhilarate someone is to make them feel very happy and excited, which is to thrill them.

clue.text: Begrudge eating sirloin regularly? Tough!

indicators.note: the word for begrudge takes the alternate letters inside, as if eating them

parts.note: to begrudge is to resent

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of sirloin, the second, fourth and sixth

explanation.surface: A diner resents chewing their sirloin, which is tough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of 'sirloin', and 'eating' puts them inside. 'Tough' looks like chewy steak, but it means hardy.
explanation.definitionFit: A resilient person is tough and able to recover quickly from setbacks.

clue.text: Do this at the butcher's and lose your job!

definitions.text: Do this at the butcher's and lose your job!

parts.words: Do this at the butcher's and lose your job!
parts.note: a customer at a butcher's might literally buy a cut of meat, while the idiom means being sacked

explanation.surface: A warning to a butcher's customer that buying meat could cost them their job.
explanation.walkthrough: At the butcher's it means collecting a pork or lamb chop; as an idiom it means being dismissed.
explanation.definitionFit: This idiom means being fired or axed from employment, and literally describes buying meat.

clue.text: Bridge player could be Dutch champion

parts.note: East, abbreviated E, is one of the four players at bridge
old Dutch is Cockney slang for a wife, from Duchess of Fife

explanation.surface: A card player might turn out to be a Dutch champion.
explanation.walkthrough: At bridge the four players are named North, South, East and West. 'Dutch' looks like a nationality, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'Duchess of Fife' means wife.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a cause is to adopt and support it, which is to champion it.

clue.text: Rope in cracking old man

indicators.note: in cracks open the word for father, sitting inside it

parts.note: pater is old-fashioned slang for father, one's old man

explanation.surface: Someone talks about roping in an elderly man who is cracking up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracking' signals the container. 'Rope' looks like a verb, as in rope in, but it is a noun; 'old man' is the old public-school word for father.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter is a rope attached to the bow of a small boat, used for tying it up.

clue.text: Stage actress is disheartened

indicators.note: losing heart means the two central letters of the surname go

parts.note: Meryl Streep is a famous actress

explanation.surface: A theatre actress feels low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is disheartened' takes RE, the middle letters, out of STREEP. 'Stage' looks like theatre, but it is the definition, as in a step or phase.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage in a process is one step of it, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Person tearing after street entertainer

indicators.note: after puts the tearer after the abbreviation

parts.note: a ripper is one who rips or tears

explanation.surface: Someone rushing off after a street performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tearing' looks like rushing, but here it means ripping.
explanation.definitionFit: A striptease artist is a kind of entertainer who undresses for the audience.

clue.text: Paddy drinks up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards, reversed

parts.note: ports are fortified wines, drinks

explanation.surface: An Irishman knocks back his drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses PORTS in this down entry. 'Paddy' looks like a name for an Irishman, but it means a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for a sulk or bad temper, as in throwing a wobbly.

clue.text: Religious leader is a timid person mostly

indicators.note: mostly means all but the final letter of the word is used

parts.note: a rabbit is slang for a timid or unskilled person

explanation.surface: A cleric is a nervous sort, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of RABBIT, slang for a timid or poor player.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish religious leader and teacher of the law.

clue.text: Learner that is outwardly least diligent

indicators.note: the Latin phrase sits outwardly, around the learner

parts.note: id est, Latin for that is, gives the abbreviation i.e.
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A student who is, frankly, the laziest of the lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outwardly' puts the Latin phrase round the learner. Taking the outer letters of 'least' tempts, but that leaves nothing to build the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of a word for lazy means the most lazy, the least diligent.

clue.text: 64 for one having lost opener, with runs for Hick

indicators.note: with puts the runs alongside the rest

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: the word for 64 loses its first letter, its opener

parts.note: 64 is four times four times four, an example of a cube

explanation.surface: A cricket scorecard: 64 for one wicket, the opening batsman out, and Hick scoring runs.
explanation.walkthrough: '64 for one' and 'opener' read as cricket, and Graeme Hick was an England batsman; but 64 is a CUBE, which 'having lost opener' cuts to UBE.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are American slang for an unsophisticated country person, a yokel or bumpkin.

clue.text: Sounds like you try nursing a beer to keep one excited

indicators.note: the assembled letters keep the numeral one inside them
the pair of pieces holds the drink between them, as one nurses a glass
Sounds like says the next word is replaced by a letter said the same way

parts.note: the letter U is said the same as you
to hear a case is to try it in court
a pint is a measure of beer
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone advises nursing a beer to stay cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounds like' turns 'you' into U; 'nursing' wraps the pair round the drink, and 'to keep' then sets I inside, making HEAIR at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Being elated and in a state of excitement is a sense of the idiom, alongside undecided.

clue.text: Opera North cuts cost with one attempt, right?

indicators.note: the compass letter cuts into the word for cost

parts.note: the cost of something is its price
I is the Roman numeral for one
a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: Opera North, a touring company, trims its costs by trying again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuts' puts N inside PRICE. Opera North is an English opera company based in Leeds, but here 'Opera' is the definition and 'North' gives N.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Borodin's Russian opera about a twelfth-century prince, so it is an example of an opera.

clue.text: Part of theatre encompassing box?

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A theatre box seat is part of the auditorium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a theatre box, but it is the evergreen shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: Box is an evergreen shrub or small tree, so it is an example of the wider category.
